newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia death squads blamed for 11 more killings.
newsitem.headline: Colombia death squads blamed for 11 more killings.

text.p: Eleven people died in two separate attacks over the weekend as killing by suspected paramilitary death squads continued across northern Colombia, police said on Sunday.
The murders were the latest in a series of violent incidents that claimed more than 60 lives in the last three weeks.

In an interview published on Sunday in the El Colombiano regional newspaper, one of Colombia's paramilitary leaders claimed he was helping the government reclaim areas of the country which had been dominated by leftist guerrillas.

He added that he hoped that not all those killed in recent paramilitary massacres had been innocent victims, and said his organisation operated with the financial and moral backing of the local inhabitants.

The publication of the interview coincided with the discovery of the bullet-pierced bodies of a woman and four young men on the outskirts of the northwest city of Medellin. Police said all had their hands tied behind their backs.
In San Alberto, in northern Cesar province, heavily-armed men dragged six peasants from their homes and shot them in the town square about midday on Saturday, police said.
"We are still looking for leads on these killings but this area has suffered problems with right-wing paramilitaries," a police spokeswoman said.
In the El Colombiano article, Carlos Castano, head of the so-called Peasant Self-defence Group of Cordoba and Uraba, denied claims that Colombia's paramilitaries were right-wing extremists.
"The State is sometimes unable to fulfil its responsibilities and look after our safety... The last right we will lose is the right to defend ourselves using our own means," Castano said.

Paramilitary death squads were the subject of a hard-hitting report by New York-based Human Rights Watch last month which claimed they were linked to the army in a systematic "dirty war" against leftist guerrillas. Castano told El Colombiano that his organisation enjoyed tacit support from middle-ranking army officers but denied any concrete link.
The paramilitary chieftain admitted partial responsibility for some massacres but did not specify which.
"Innocent people die; of course they do. I'm not pretending they don't. In war they do die... but let's hope it has not just been innocent people that have died," he said.
